prompt: Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon. They are an example of:
options: Isotopes (different neutron count)
Allotropes (or polymorphs)
Isomers (different connectivity)
Different elements entirely
explanation: Diamond and graphite are allotropes — different crystal structures of the same element. Allotropy is the term for elements; polymorphism is the broader term covering compounds. Either term applies to carbon.

prompt: Why does pure iron transform from BCC (α) to FCC (γ) at 912 °C?
options: Atoms gain electrons at high temperature
FCC has lower free energy at 912–1394 °C
Bonds change from metallic to covalent
The transformation is purely magnetic
correctAnswer: FCC has lower free energy at 912–1394 °C
explanation: Above 912 °C, the FCC arrangement minimises Gibbs free energy thanks to favourable phonon entropy. The transformation is reversed on cooling, and switches the carbon solubility (austenite holds far more carbon than ferrite) — the foundation of all steel heat treatment.

prompt: What happens to ordinary metallic tin at temperatures well below 13.2 °C?
options: It becomes harder and stronger over time
Slow change to brittle grey α-tin (tin pest)
It evaporates into the surrounding air
It oxidises to tin(II) oxide on its surface
correctAnswer: Slow change to brittle grey α-tin (tin pest)
explanation: Tin pest is the spontaneous β → α transition below 13.2 °C, turning the metal into crumbling grey powder. Lead-free electronics solder (mostly tin) revived concerns; small additions of bismuth or antimony are used to suppress the transition.

prompt: A single sheet of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal lattice is called _____.
explanation: Graphene is a single 2-D atomic layer of sp²-bonded carbon. Its isolation by Geim and Novoselov (Nobel Prize 2010) opened a new field of two-dimensional materials with remarkable electronic and mechanical properties.

prompt: Match each carbon allotrope to its bonding/structure:
explanation: Carbon's flexibility comes from its ability to form sp, sp², and sp³ hybrids. Each yields a distinct macroscopic material — from the hardest natural solid (diamond) to a soft layered conductor (graphite) to molecular soccer balls.

prompt: Which is a defining feature of a first-order phase transition?
options: Absence of any latent heat at the transition
Discontinuous jump in entropy and volume
No coexistence of phases at the boundary
Always reversible without hysteresis
correctAnswer: Discontinuous jump in entropy and volume
explanation: First-order transitions involve a discontinuity in the first derivative of Gibbs free energy — meaning a sudden change in entropy and volume — and require absorption or release of latent heat L = TΔS. Melting and boiling are familiar first-order transitions.

prompt: The ferromagnetic-to-paramagnetic transition of iron at 770 °C (Curie point) is:
options: First order, with substantial latent heat
Continuous (second order); magnetisation drops
Discontinuous in volume but not entropy
Identical in mechanism to ordinary melting
explanation: The Curie transition is continuous: magnetisation drops smoothly to zero at T_c. Heat capacity diverges (a 'lambda' anomaly), but there is no latent heat and no two-phase coexistence. It is the textbook example of a continuous transition with broken symmetry.

prompt: An order parameter is:
options: A universal constant of nature like c
Zero when symmetric, grows when broken
Identical to a transition's latent heat value
Always temperature itself, by definition
correctAnswer: Zero when symmetric, grows when broken
explanation: Order parameters quantify the degree of broken symmetry: magnetisation for ferromagnets, density difference for fluids near the critical point, sublattice ordering for alloys, etc. They underpin Landau theory and the modern classification of phase transitions.

prompt: The fact that very different physical systems share the same critical exponents near a continuous phase transition is called _____.
explanation: Universality is one of the deepest results in statistical mechanics: a magnet at its Curie point and a fluid at its liquid-gas critical point obey the same exponents because they belong to the same universality class. Wilson's renormalisation group (Nobel 1982) explained why.

prompt: Match each transition to its order:

pairs.left: Liquid helium becoming superfluid at 2.17 K

explanation: First-order transitions involve coexistence and latent heat (melting). Continuous transitions feature smooth order-parameter growth and divergent susceptibilities (Curie, lambda). Ehrenfest's two-class scheme is a useful starting taxonomy for the much richer modern picture.

prompt: A displacive phase transition involves:
options: Bonds breaking and reforming completely
Small atomic displacements; bonds preserved
Long-distance diffusion of many atoms
Only molecular rearrangements in liquids
explanation: Displacive transitions involve only small (sub-bond) atomic motions. The α-quartz to β-quartz inversion at 573 °C is the canonical example: tetrahedra tilt, but no Si-O bond breaks. Such transitions are fast and reversible.

prompt: Why is a reconstructive transition usually slow and prone to kinetic freezing?
options: Because it requires extremely low temperatures
Bonds must break; atoms migrate over distance
Because reconstructive only occurs at high pressure
Reconstructive means quick atomic rearrangement
correctAnswer: Bonds must break; atoms migrate over distance
explanation: Reconstructive transitions topologically reorganise the crystal — bonds rupture and reconnect. The activation energy is large; below a kinetic threshold the transition cannot proceed even if it is thermodynamically favoured. Diamond at room temperature is a classic frozen example.

prompt: At room temperature and 1 atm, diamond is:
options: The thermodynamic ground state of carbon
Metastable; graphite is more stable but frozen
An entirely different element from graphite
A gas under standard ambient conditions
correctAnswer: Metastable; graphite is more stable but frozen
explanation: At ambient conditions graphite has a slightly lower free energy than diamond, but the diamond → graphite transformation requires breaking every C-C bond and rearranging into sheets. The activation energy is so high that diamonds last unchanged for billions of years.

prompt: A phase that is not the thermodynamic ground state but is stable on practical timescales because the conversion is kinetically frozen is called _____.
explanation: Metastable phases sit in a local free-energy minimum, not the global one, but the barrier to reach the true ground state is too high to cross at ordinary temperatures. Engineering alloys depend heavily on holding metastable microstructures stable enough to use.

prompt: Match each transition to its character:

pairs.right: Reconstructive — kinetically frozen, diamond is metastable

explanation: Displacive transitions like quartz inversion are virtually instantaneous and reversible. Reconstructive transitions break and reform bonds; they may proceed slowly (quartz → cristobalite at high T) or be effectively frozen (diamond at room T).

prompt: A martensitic transformation is best described as:
options: A diffusion-controlled equilibrium reaction
Diffusionless cooperative shear of the lattice
A simple equilibrium melting transition
An ordinary magnetic ordering transition
correctAnswer: Diffusionless cooperative shear of the lattice
explanation: Martensitic transformations involve cooperative, diffusionless shears: each atom moves less than a bond length and no long-range diffusion occurs. The transformation can therefore proceed at speeds approaching the speed of sound, even at very low temperatures.

prompt: What makes martensite in quenched steel hard and brittle?
options: Very high cobalt or tungsten content
Carbon trapped in BCT lattice with fine plates
A coarse-grained ferrite microstructure with large grains
Soft cementite particles in the bulk material
correctAnswer: Carbon trapped in BCT lattice with fine plates
explanation: Quenching denies carbon time to diffuse out of austenite during the γ → α' shear. The carbon is locked into a distorted body-centred tetragonal lattice, and the resulting fine plate microstructure obstructs dislocations heavily. Together they yield the high hardness and low ductility characteristic of as-quenched steel.

prompt: Which alloy is the basis of most commercial shape-memory devices?
options: Cu-Sn (bronze)
NiTi (nitinol)
Fe-C (steel)
Pb-Sn (solder)
explanation: Nitinol (~50:50 NiTi) undergoes a reversible martensitic transformation between a high-symmetry austenite and a low-symmetry martensite. This underlies both the thermal shape-memory effect and stress-induced superelasticity used in stents, eyewear, and orthodontic wires.

prompt: The reversible recovery of large strains (~8 %) in nitinol above its austenite-finish temperature is called _____.
explanation: Superelasticity (or pseudoelasticity) is the stress-induced version of the shape-memory effect. Stress drives a reversible austenite → martensite transformation; on unloading, austenite re-forms and the strain disappears. The strain comes from a phase transformation, not bond stretching.

prompt: Match each shape-memory feature to its mechanism:

pairs.right: Reversion of low-symmetry martensite to high-symmetry austenite
Stress-induced martensite that reverts on unloading
Locking in a new shape that 'remembers' the previous one

explanation: All three features come from one underlying physics: a reversible martensitic transformation. The macroscopic richness — shape memory, superelasticity, training — emerges from the interplay of temperature, stress, and crystallographic variant selection within the martensite phase.

prompt: A glass is best described as:
options: A crystal containing many vacancies
Non-crystalline solid from quenched liquid
An ordinary two-phase mixture of solids
A simple pure metal in solid form
explanation: Glasses retain the disordered atomic arrangement of the liquid but lose mobility — they are 'frozen liquids'. Silicates, polymers, chalcogenides, and certain alloys can all be quenched into glassy states.

prompt: The glass transition temperature T_g depends on:
options: External pressure only
Cooling rate (slower → lower T_g)
Underlying crystal symmetry of the parent
Atomic mass of the constituent elements
explanation: T_g is a kinetic transition: the temperature at which the relaxation time of the liquid exceeds the experimental timescale. Slower cooling allows atoms more time to find low-energy configurations before locking, lowering T_g. There is no unique thermodynamic T_g.

prompt: Why does a natural rubber ball shatter like glass after being dipped in liquid nitrogen (−196 °C)?
options: It crystallises completely and immediately
Drops below T_g; chains lose mobility
It oxidises rapidly upon prolonged cold exposure
It loses elasticity due to ambient pressure drop
correctAnswer: Drops below T_g; chains lose mobility
explanation: Above T_g (~−70 °C for natural rubber), polymer chains can wiggle freely, giving entropic elasticity. Below T_g, segmental motion freezes and the material behaves as a glassy solid. Almost all polymer mechanical behaviour is a story of how the service temperature compares to T_g.

prompt: Bulk metallic glasses, like Zr-Cu-Ni-Ti-Be alloys, became practical in the 1990s because they can be quenched into the glassy state at relatively _____ cooling rates.
explanation: Pure metals require ~10⁹ K/s to glass and produce only thin ribbons. Multi-component bulk metallic glass alloys can be quenched at ~1 K/s — slow enough to cast bulk parts. Their high strength, elasticity, and corrosion resistance opened a new class of engineering metals.

prompt: Match each material to its approximate glass transition temperature:
explanation: T_g spans hundreds of degrees across material families. Silicate glasses are rigid up to many hundreds of °C. Engineering thermoplastics like polycarbonate are rigid at room temperature but soften before 150 °C. Rubbers are deliberately formulated below room temperature to remain elastic in service.
